key_terms.meaning: An ordered list x₁, x₂, …, x_T whose length T varies from one example to the next; the order carries meaning.
The whole sequence gives one label, as in a review → positive or negative.
One output tag per input step, T inputs → T outputs, as in part-of-speech tagging.
A source sequence of length T produces a target sequence of a different length U.
A vector of numbers the RNN carries forward from earlier steps; h_t = tanh(W_x x_t + W_h h_{t−1} + b).
The same W_x, W_h and b are used at every time step, so the model size does not grow with T.
Drawing the shared cell once per time step as a chain, turning the loop into a feed-forward graph.
Backpropagation on the unfolded graph; the gradient for a shared weight is the sum of its gradients at all steps.
Repeated multiplication by W_h and tanh′ shrinks the gradient as it travels back, so far steps learn almost nothing.
The same repeated product grows the gradient instead; losses jump to NaN or Inf.
If the gradient norm exceeds a threshold c, rescale it to length c before the update.
A sigmoid layer producing values in (0,1) that scale how much information passes.
The LSTM's memory line, updated additively: C_t = f_t ⊙ C_{t−1} + i_t ⊙ g_t.
A gated cell with two gates (reset and update) and no separate cell state.
One network reads the source into a context vector; a second network generates the target token by token.
The encoder's final hidden state, a fixed-size summary of the whole input sequence.
A shallow model that learns dense word vectors by predicting context from a word (skip-gram) or a word from its context (CBOW).
A model of P(w_t | w₁ … w_{t−1}); its quality is scored by perplexity.

takeaways: Sequence problems differ by shape — many-to-one, same-length many-to-many, and sequence-to-sequence — not by the kind of data.
An RNN is one cell reused at every step, so the number of parameters stays fixed while the sequence length changes.
Unfolding turns the loop into a chain; that chain is what makes backpropagation through time possible.
BPTT sums gradients from every time step into the same shared weights, which is exactly why long sequences are hard to train.
The vanishing gradient is a product of many small factors; gated cells replace that product with an additive path and a sigmoid gate that learns to stay near 1.
Exploding gradients are cheap to fix — clip the norm — while vanishing gradients need an architectural change such as LSTM or GRU gates.
An encoder–decoder splits the job in two: read the whole input, then write the output one token at a time.
Word2vec learns meaning from co-occurrence alone; similar words end up with similar vectors, and vector arithmetic starts to make sense.
Language modelling, translation and image captioning share the same recurrent stack; only the encoder and the output head change.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually graded on the unfolded diagram with correct shapes, the BPTT gradient sum written out, the LSTM gate equations with the additive cell state, and the encoder–decoder data flow.

bank.q: Explain the three shapes of sequence learning problems with one example each, and say what the loss looks like in each case.
outline: Many-to-one: one label for the whole sequence, loss on the last hidden state (sentiment).
Many-to-many same length: one tag per step, loss summed over T steps (POS tagging, NER).
Many-to-many sequence-to-sequence: lengths differ, loss summed over the target steps only (translation).
Note that the network can be identical; only the output head and the loss change.
Mention variable length and padding or bucketing.

bank.q: Draw an RNN cell and its unfolding over three time steps. Write the forward equations and explain why the weights are shared.
outline: h_t = tanh(W_x x_t + W_h h_{t−1} + b), y_t = softmax(W_y h_t).
Define each symbol with its shape: x_t is d×1, W_x is k×d, W_h is k×k.
Unfolded graph: same cell drawn T times, h_{t−1} → h_t edge between copies.
Weight sharing keeps parameter count independent of T and lets one pattern be learned at any position.
The stored hidden state is the only thing passed between steps at inference.

bank.q: State the LSTM forward equations for the forget, input, output gates and the cell state, and define every symbol.
outline: f_t = σ(W_f [h_{t−1}, x_t] + b_f), i_t, o_t similarly.
Candidate g_t = tanh(W_g [h_{t−1}, x_t] + b_g).
C_t = f_t ⊙ C_{t−1} + i_t ⊙ g_t; h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(C_t).
σ is the logistic sigmoid giving values in (0,1); ⊙ is element-wise product.
Say what each gate does: erase, write, expose.

bank.q: What is the vanishing gradient problem in an RNN? Show where the repeated product comes from and why gating helps.
outline: ∂h_t/∂h_{t−1} contains W_hᵀ diag(tanh′(·)); the chain over T steps multiplies these.
Products of many factors below 1 shrink to zero; above 1 they explode.
Effect: the model cannot learn dependencies spanning many steps.
Gating gives an additive path ∂C_t/∂C_{t−1} = f_t, so the gate can hold near 1 and keep the gradient alive.
Mention that this is mitigation, not a cure.

bank.q: A character-level RNN is trained on a 50-symbol alphabet with a hidden size of 128. Work out the parameter count of the cell and of the output layer.
outline: Input weights: 128 × 50 = 6400; hidden weights: 128 × 128 = 16384; bias 128.
Cell total 22,912 parameters.
Output layer 50 × 128 + 50 = 6450.
Total about 29,362 — and it does not change when the sequence length grows.
Contrast with a fully connected layer over a fixed window, where it would.

bank.q: Describe how you would train a sequence-to-sequence translator for English to Tamil. Cover data preparation, teacher forcing, decoding and evaluation.
outline: Tokenise both sides, build vocabularies, append start and end tokens, pad batches.
Encoder reads the source and its final state becomes the context vector.
Decoder input at each step is the previous target token during training (teacher forcing); the loss is cross-entropy on target tokens only, padding masked.
Decoding at test time: greedy or beam search, feeding back the model's own output.
Evaluate with BLEU; note exposure bias from teacher forcing.
Mention clipping and gradient accumulation for long batches.

bank.q: Explain how word2vec skip-gram is trained with negative sampling. Give the objective and say why negative sampling is used.
outline: For a centre word w and a true context word c, maximise σ(u_c · v_w).
For each of k sampled noise words c′, maximise σ(−u_{c′} · v_w).
Objective: Σ log σ(u_c·v_w) + Σ log σ(−u_{c′}·v_w).
Full softmax over a 10⁵-word vocabulary is too expensive, so K negative pairs replace it.
Negative words drawn from a unigram distribution raised to the 3/4 power.
Resulting vectors show semantic similarity and analogy structure.

bank.q: Show how an image captioning system is built from a CNN and an RNN. Label the shape of every tensor at the join.
outline: CNN (for example ResNet) turns the image into a feature map; global pooling gives a vector of size D.
That vector seeds the RNN's first hidden state, or is fed as x₀ at every step.
The word sequence is embedded to dimension E and fed step by step; the output head is a softmax over the vocabulary.
Trained with cross-entropy using teacher forcing on caption–image pairs.
Decoding with greedy or beam search gives the caption.

bank.q: Compare LSTM and GRU cells: equations, parameter count and when you would choose one over the other.
outline: Two gates and no separate cell state, so fewer parameters — roughly three quarters of an LSTM of the same width.
LSTM's separate cell state gives a cleaner additive path and better very-long memory.
GRU trains faster on small data; differences are often small and data-dependent.
Both are replaced by attention or transformers when the sequence is long or the data is large.

bank.q: A deep RNN shows smooth training loss but the validation loss suddenly jumps to NaN. Diagnose the cause and list the remedies in order.
outline: NaN loss points to exploding gradients, not overfitting.
Confirm by logging the gradient norm per step.
First fix: clip the gradient norm to a threshold such as 1 to 5.
Then lower the learning rate, and consider a smaller hidden size.
Architectural: use LSTM or GRU, add layer normalisation.
Data: shorter truncated backprop windows, batch-size sanity check.

bank.q: Why does a plain encoder–decoder fail on very long sentences, and how does attention change the picture? Refer to query, key and value.
outline: The whole source is squeezed into one fixed-size context vector; detail is lost as length grows.
Attention keeps every encoder state and lets the decoder look back at all of them.
Query from the decoder state, keys and values from the encoder states.
Scores q·k scored, softmaxed into weights, then the weighted sum of values is the context.
Gradients reach distant source positions directly, shortening the path.
Mention multi-head attention and the move to transformers.

bank.q: Explain backpropagation through time in full: the unfolded graph, the gradient recursion, and truncated BPTT.
outline: Unfold to T steps; each copy has its own local gradient but shares weights.
∂L/∂W_h = Σ_t ∂L_t/∂W_h, summed over steps because of weight sharing.
Recursion: δ_t = (W_hᵀ δ_{t+1}) ⊙ (1 − h_t²) + output term.
Cost is O(T) memory and time; forward states must be kept for the backward pass.
Truncated BPTT splits long sequences into windows and carries the state forward.
Link the recursion's repeated product to vanishing and exploding gradients.

bank.q: Word embeddings learned on a news corpus are used in a hospital's report classifier. Discuss what can go wrong and how you would evaluate the vectors before trusting them.
outline: Domain shift: clinical vocabulary and abbreviations are unseen or wrongly placed.
Bias encoded from the corpus: gender or caste associations carried into the vectors.
Out-of-vocabulary words get no vector; subword models reduce this.
Evaluate on intrinsic tasks (similarity, analogy) and extrinsic tasks (the classifier itself).
Inspect nearest neighbours of sensitive words.
Fine-tune on in-domain text or use contextual models instead of static vectors.

glossary.def: One unit of a sequence — a character, a word or a subword piece.
The vector an RNN passes from one step to the next, summarising everything seen so far.
Redrawing a recurrent network as one copy of the cell per time step, joined in a chain.
Backpropagation applied to the unfolded RNN graph, summing gradients over time steps into the shared weights.
Running BPTT on fixed-length windows of a long sequence and carrying the hidden state forward between windows.
A gradient that shrinks toward zero as it travels back through many steps, so early steps barely learn.
A gradient that grows without bound through many steps, producing NaN or Inf in training.
Rescaling the gradient to a maximum norm before the update, the standard cure for exploding gradients.
A sigmoid layer whose outputs between 0 and 1 scale how much of a signal passes through.
The LSTM's long-term memory line, changed additively by the forget and input gates.
Decides what fraction of the previous cell state to keep.
Decides how much of the new candidate memory to write into the cell state.
Decides how much of the cell state to expose as the hidden state.
Gated recurrent unit; a two-gate cell with a reset gate and an update gate and no separate cell state.
The network that reads the input sequence and produces a representation of it.
The network that produces the output sequence one token at a time from the encoder's representation.
A fixed-size vector summarising the input sequence, passed from encoder to decoder.
Feeding the true previous target token to the decoder during training instead of its own prediction.
A dense learned vector for a word, in which distance reflects similarity of use.
The word2vec variant that predicts context words from one centre word.
Continuous bag of words; the word2vec variant that predicts a centre word from its context words.
Training shortcut that replaces the full softmax with a few true and a few random noise pairs.
The exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per token; lower is better.
Decoding that keeps the k best partial sequences at each step instead of only the best one.
A weighted lookup where a query is compared with keys and the weights are applied to values.
Generating a sentence that describes an image, usually with a CNN encoder and a recurrent decoder.
